snip.t: Immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor).
Positive rheumatoid factor or anti‑CCP in serum (lab): Serologic confirmation — Autoantibodies formed against Fc portion of IgG (RF) or citrullinated peptides (anti‑CCP).
| RF (IgM) | Presence of rheumatoid factor | Positive in many RA patients but also in other diseases; high titres suggest severe disease |
| Rheumatoid arthritis | Symmetrical small‑joint arthritis, morning stiffness | Presence of erosions on X‑ray, rheumatoid factor/anti‑CCP positivity, lack of photosensitive rash. |
| Acute rheumatoid flare | Symmetrical polyarthritis, morning stiffness >1 h, rheumatoid nodules. | Positive rheumatoid factor/anti‑CCP; erosive changes on X‑ray; no MSU crystals. |
| Rheumatoid arthritis | Symmetrical polyarthritis, prolonged morning stiffness >1 h, rheumatoid nodules | Positive rheumatoid factor/anti‑CCP, erosive changes on X‑ray, systemic features |

qs.q: A young patient presents with symmetrical polyarthritis, intermittent fever lasting at least 2 weeks with spikes on at least 3 consecutive days, and a salmon-pink maculopapular rash on the proximal limbs and torso. Rheumatoid factor and ANA are negative, but ferritin is elevated. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Adult onset still disease requires arthritis involving more than one joint, intermittent fever for at least 2 weeks with spikes on 3 consecutive days, and extra-articular manifestations such as a salmon-pink rash and elevated ferritin with negative RF and ANA. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis begins before the age of 16, whereas adult onset still disease can occur in older populations.

qs.q: A patient evaluated for infective endocarditis is found to have microscopic hematuria, elevated ESR, and a positive rheumatoid factor. What is the primary underlying pathological mechanism for the glomerulonephritis seen in this patient?
qs.e: Glomerulonephritis in infective endocarditis is an immunological manifestation driven by the deposition of immune complexes in the renal glomeruli, often accompanied by elevated rheumatoid factor. This differs from renal infarction, which is caused by large septic emboli.

qs.q: A patient with a known connective tissue disease is evaluated for a slow-onset interstitial lung disease. Serology shows positive rheumatoid factor and antinuclear factor, but no specific circulating marker for the primary lung disease exists. Which hallmark radiological sign appears in advanced stages of this fibrotic process?
qs.e: Advanced stages of pulmonary fibrosis, such as IPF, feature a honeycombing appearance on chest radiography and HRCT (subpleural cysts and reticular pattern). Pleural plaques are more typical of asbestos exposure rather than autoimmune-related fibrosis.

qs.q: A 60-year-old woman has 20 years of crippling hand and foot arthritis with ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are markedly elevated. Rectal biopsy shows Congo red-positive amorphous deposits. Most likely precursor protein?
qs.e: Rheumatoid arthritis → chronic inflammation → elevated SAA (serum amyloid-associated protein) → secondary (reactive, AA) amyloidosis depositing in multiple organs including the rectum.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an IgM (or IgA) autoantibody against the Fc portion of IgG, found in many autoimmune and infectious diseases. It helps diagnose rheumatoid arthritis but is not disease‑specific.

sections.p: RF is an autoantibody that forms immune complexes, contributing to joint inflammation. It is measured by nephelometry or latex agglutination; a titre >20 IU/mL is usually considered positive.
b: Positive RF supports rheumatoid arthritis (RA) but must be interpreted with clinical picture and other tests.

t.b: Does the patient have circulating anti‑IgG antibodies? Positive result suggests autoimmune disease; negative does not exclude RA.
Is there a more specific marker for RA? Positive anti‑CCP with RF increases likelihood of erosive disease.
Is there systemic lupus or other connective‑tissue disease? Negative ANA with positive RF leans toward RA.

sections.p: RA severity is staged by joint damage (radiographs) and functional status (DAS28, HAQ). High RF titres correlate with more aggressive disease and erosions.
b: RF titre >3× upper limit predicts rapid radiographic progression.

sections.p: RF can arise from several conditions; the most common is rheumatoid arthritis, followed by chronic infections and other autoimmune disorders.
b: Rheumatoid arthritis – primary autoimmune cause.
Chronic hepatitis C – immune complex formation.
HIV infection – polyclonal B‑cell activation.
Tuberculosis – chronic antigenic stimulation (relevant in low‑resource settings).
Other autoimmune diseases (Sjogren’s, systemic sclerosis).

sections.p: Patients with RF‑positive RA present with symmetric polyarthritis of small joints, morning stiffness >1 hour, and possible rheumatoid nodules.
b: Swollen, tender metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.
Morning stiffness improving with activity.
Systemic features: fatigue, low‑grade fever.

sections.p: Beyond RF, a combination of serology, imaging, and functional scores confirms diagnosis and guides treatment.
b: X‑ray of hands/feet for erosions.
Ultrasound or MRI to detect early synovitis.
Baseline CBC, liver/kidney function before therapy.

t.b: Are there erosions or joint space narrowing? Positive findings confirm structural damage and stage disease.
Is there active synovitis? Detects inflammation when X‑ray is normal.
Are baseline organ functions safe for DMARDs? Abnormal results may limit drug choices.

sections.p: Uncontrolled RF‑positive RA can lead to irreversible joint destruction, cardiovascular disease, and extra‑articular manifestations.
b: Rapidly progressive erosive arthritis.
Seropositive RA increases risk of myocardial infarction.
Rheumatoid nodules, pulmonary fibrosis, vasculitis.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; for RA, start disease‑modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and consider biologics if response is inadequate.
b: Methotrexate – first‑line DMARD; reduces immune activation.
Sulfasalazine or leflunomide – alternatives when methotrexate contraindicated.
TNF‑α inhibitors (e.g., etanercept) – for refractory disease; avoid in active infection.
Short‑course NSAIDs or low‑dose steroids for symptom control.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of disease activity, drug toxicity, and comorbidities is essential.
b: Assess DAS28 every 3–6 months.
Screen for cardiovascular risk annually.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.

sections.p: Conditions that can also show positive RF or similar joint symptoms.
b: Systemic lupus erythematosus – often ANA positive, low RF.
Psoriatic arthritis – asymmetric, skin lesions, usually RF negative.
Parvovirus B19 infection – acute symmetric arthritis, transient RF.

sections.p: RF may be falsely positive or negative, leading to diagnostic errors.
b: Low‑titer RF in healthy older adults can be misinterpreted as disease.
Early RA may have negative RF; rely on clinical picture and anti‑CCP.
Chronic infections (HCV) can produce high RF without arthritis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe joint swelling, fever, or inability to move a limb – possible septic arthritis; new chest pain or shortness of breath in RA – risk of pulmonary involvement.

faq.q: Is a positive RF enough to diagnose rheumatoid arthritis?
faq.a: No; RF must be combined with clinical findings and preferably anti‑CCP positivity.

faq.q: Why can hepatitis C cause a high RF?
faq.a: Chronic viral antigenemia stimulates B‑cells to produce IgM RF, forming cryoglobulin complexes.

faq.q: Can RF be negative in established RA?
faq.a: Yes; up to 20 % of RA patients are seronegative, especially early disease.
